content: 📌 Public Library
The library reopened last month.
The library now provides:

a comfortable magazine-reading areaa larger collection of books about [ _____ ]a new collection concerning local [ _____ ]a community room for meetings, which members may also use to [ _____ ]a new fiction collection for [ _____ ]
For younger children:
At the next Science Club meeting, experiments will use items found in the [ _____ ].In the Reading Challenge, children read six books during the holidays.
For adults:

This Friday, a local writer discusses a novel inspired by a real [ _____ ].IT assistance is available on Tuesday, and no [ _____ ] is required.People over sixty can receive free checks of blood [ _____ ] and cholesterol.
Other information:
The library shop sells wall charts, cards and [ _____ ].Free [ _____ ] is provided during evenings and weekends.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two friends discussing the facilities and activities at a recently reopened public library. First, you have some time to look at questions one to four. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to four.
[00:51] SUSIE: Hello.
[00:51] PAUL: Hi Susie, it's Paul. How are things? Are you enjoying the new job? You're at the library now, aren't you?
[01:00] SUSIE: Yes, I began when the library reopened last month and I'm really enjoying it.
[01:07] PAUL: Carol and I have actually been planning to become members for some time.

[01:11] SUSIE: You should. Membership is free and the rebuilt library provides all kinds of facilities. It isn't simply somewhere to borrow books. There's a comfortable seating area, for example, where visitors can read the magazines.
[01:27] SUSIE: Some people stay there all morning.
[01:30] PAUL: I wish I had enough spare time to do that.
[01:33] SUSIE: You must be extremely busy at the moment with the children and everything else.
[01:38] PAUL: We are. Still, we hope to take a holiday this summer, perhaps in Greece.
[01:45] SUSIE: Then you should look at our travel section. It's much larger than before. I can't remember whether we have books specifically about Greece, but I expect we do.
[01:56] PAUL: Good. Carol is also preparing a project for the history class she teaches. It's about daily life in the town a century ago. Would the library have anything useful?
[02:09] SUSIE: Yes. We've created a new collection about local history covering both the town and the surrounding area.
[02:18] PAUL: I'll tell her. That kind of material isn't always available online. The old library had a separate reference room, which was a wonderfully quiet place.

[02:31] SUSIE: The reference books are now in the main library. However, we have a community room that organizations can hire for meetings. When no meeting is taking place, members may use it to study.
[02:44] PAUL: I could certainly use that. Finding a quiet place at home is sometimes impossible.
[02:50] SUSIE: I can't remember the ages of your son and daughter. There's now a special fiction section for teenagers, although they may still be too young for it.
[03:01] PAUL: Yes, they are.
[03:05] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions five to ten. Now listen and answer questions five to ten.
[03:52] SUSIE: We do organize plenty of activities for younger children, though.
[03:55] PAUL: Such as?
[03:58] SUSIE: One is the science club. At its next meeting, the children will carry out experiments using ordinary things found in the kitchen, such as flour and sugar.
[04:10] PAUL: They might enjoy that.

[04:12] SUSIE: There's also a children's competition called the reading challenge. It begins after the school term finishes. Participants read six books during the holidays and receive a certificate if they complete the challenge.
[04:28] PAUL: That should stop them becoming bored during the break.

[04:31] SUSIE: That's the intention. We arrange events for adults as well. This Friday, a local writer named Tanya Streep will discuss her new novel, Catch the Mouse. The story is based on a crime that really happened in this area many years ago.
[04:48] PAUL: We're busy on Friday, but I'll look for the novel.

[04:53] SUSIE: This next service may not be relevant to you, but members can get help with information technology. Many older people come because they want to improve their computer skills. Support is offered on Tuesday mornings, and there's no need to make an appointment. People can simply arrive.
[05:12] PAUL: My mother might find that useful. I'll mention it to her.
[05:16] SUSIE: We also provide something people don't normally associate with a library, a free health check, a hospital worker visits to measure blood sugar and cholesterol levels.
[05:29] PAUL: Really?
[05:30] SUSIE: Yes, although it's restricted to people over 60, so you don't qualify yet.
[05:37] PAUL: I'll tell my mother about that too.
[05:40] SUSIE: Let me think what else you should know. The small library shop sells wall charts, greeting cards and stamps, which means you can post a card immediately after buying it.
[05:52] PAUL: I'll bring the children at the weekend so that we can all join. One last question. I'll come by car. Is parking available?
[06:02] SUSIE: Yes. Parking is free during the evenings and at weekends.
[06:07] PAUL: Perfect. Thanks, Susie. See you.

transcript: [00:01] AUDIO: You will hear a trainer describing specialised holidays offered by BC Travel. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 17. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 17. In this part of today's training, we'll examine some of BC Travel's more specialised holidays.

[01:01] AUDIO: Tourism is a highly competitive industry, so we must understand how the market is developing. Looking first at age, travellers over 65 form an important market that has grown steadily each year. People aged 31 to 42 take the fewest holidays, and their numbers show no indication of increasing. The largest group is still those aged 16 to 30, but it has experienced the sharpest decline in recent years.

[01:34] AUDIO: By contrast, bookings among 55 to 64 year olds have risen noticeably. Demand from travellers aged 43 to 54 has remained stable rather than producing the growth we anticipated. Across almost every age group, holidays built around a specialised activity are becoming more popular. These aren't adventure holidays involving dangerous activities, such as whitewater rafting, purely for excitement.

[02:05] AUDIO: They usually feature lower risk sports or pursuits such as art and music. Nor do they necessarily offer better value than conventional holidays. They frequently cost more. However, these trips are often based away from major tourist centres.

[02:24] AUDIO: As a result, clients can learn more about local residents and customs, and many describe that cultural contact as a major benefit. Participants also develop a skill or talent, but they often say that the strongest attraction is meeting like-minded people and forming friendships that continue after the holiday. Let me give you some examples. Our painting holidays operate at four centres in France and Italy and welcome all standards, including beginners.

[02:58] AUDIO: We already have an excellent group of artists teaching the classes, several of whom have worked with us from the beginning. Five more teachers join us this year, enabling every centre to run additional classes. With cooking holidays, many companies concentrate on recipes from one country, normally the country being visited. Our programmes are different because participants prepare dishes from many nations.

[03:27] AUDIO: We also use high-quality organic ingredients, as clients now expect, and usually include some vegetarian recipes. Photography holidays are available in countries ranging from Iceland to Vietnam, giving participants access to remarkable scenery. Each group contains no more than eight people, so every client receives individual tuition. Excursions are led by qualified guides.

[03:56] AUDIO: At the end, the group holds an exhibition, allowing everyone to view the other participants' photographs and receive useful comments from the tutor. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 18 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 18 to 20. Finally, I'll describe our fitness holidays.

[04:59] AUDIO: In Ireland and Italy, we provide week-long general fitness courses for people of every age and ability. Each client first meets a trainer, and together they design a personal programme. Besides becoming fitter, participants report losing much of the stress accumulated in everyday life. Our Greek programme lasts two weeks and is intended for people who want to control their weight.

[05:27] AUDIO: It includes the expected features, such as an individual diet plan, but the most popular element is that all exercise sessions take place on the beach. Clients prefer that setting to a gym. We also run several holidays in Morocco. One of the most successful is based on mountain biking.

[05:49] AUDIO: We supply the bicycles and provide different routes for different ability levels. One version is designed specifically for families and is particularly popular. That's all I have time to cover today. Thank you very much.

content: 📌 Tourism Case Study
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two students, Natalie and Dave, discussing how to prepare a tourism case study. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
[00:52] NATALIE: Dave, I'm getting worried about our case study. I've done some reading, but I'm unclear about the process of writing one, because I missed Dr. Baker's lecture on it.
[01:03] DAVE: It's fairly straightforward. We already have our focus, tourism at the Horton Castle site, and you've begun reading about it.
[01:13] NATALIE: Yes. I found several articles and noted their main ideas.
[01:19] DAVE: Did you also record the sources of all the information?
[01:22] NATALIE: Of course. I know how frustrating it is when you forget to do that.
[01:28] DAVE: Good. We can compare our reading, then identify one particular problem or need at the site. After that, we decide whom to interview for further information.
[01:40] NATALIE: Who should we speak to? Employees at the site? And perhaps some visitors?
[01:46] DAVE: Yes, both groups. So we'll need to travel there. We could also interview people away from the castle, including city officials responsible for tourism.
[01:56] NATALIE: Then we must prepare the interview questions and arrange the times and locations. This will take quite a while?
[02:04] DAVE: It will. If possible, we should also ask interviewees to provide numerical data that can support our findings.
[02:13] NATALIE: What about photographs?
[02:15] DAVE: We already have enough. But Dr. Baker said we must ask whether we may use interviewees' names in the study, or whether they prefer to remain anonymous.
[02:26] NATALIE: I wouldn't have remembered that. Once all the material has been collected, I suppose we analyze it.

[02:34] DAVE: Exactly. We combine everything, select what directly relates to the problem, and examine it closely for patterns or regularities. Recognizing those is more important at this stage than collecting endless details and facts.
[02:50] NATALIE: And after the analysis?
[02:52] DAVE: We choose the clearest visual format for the selected data, perhaps graphs, tables, or charts.
[03:01] NATALIE: Right.

[03:02] DAVE: Writing the case study itself is mostly conventional. We introduce the problem and provide some background before moving through the main sections. What surprised me is the ending. A standard report would normally finish with proposed solutions to the identified problem.
[03:22] DAVE: A case study instead concludes with one or more questions for its readers, who decide what should be done.
[03:29] NATALIE: I hadn't realized that.
[03:34] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen, and answer questions 27 to 30.
[04:16] NATALIE: So our main issue is why Horton Castle attracts so few visitors. The interviews should tell us more, but an online report suggested that poor transport access might be one reason.

[04:33] DAVE: I saw that report, but it was written 10 years ago, when the road was in a terrible condition. The road has since been improved. The site has enough interesting features for a full day's visit, but the castle's website makes it sound dull. I think inadequate publicity may be the real problem.
[04:53] NATALIE: I agree. The website is very dry.
[04:57] DAVE: I also found a proposal for a visitor center. We could research that idea online. What information would we require?

[05:06] NATALIE: First, we'd need to know who would use it. It would help to identify visitor categories, such as school groups and retired people. But the site staff would probably have to supply those figures.
[05:20] DAVE: Since we may recommend a visitor center, we also need to examine possible difficulties. Building it would obviously require substantial investment.
[05:30] NATALIE: True, but it could be worthwhile. Because the castle is a historic site, special planning permission would be necessary, and obtaining that might be extremely difficult.
[05:43] DAVE: Especially since the only possible space is by the entrance, directly in front of the castle.
[05:51] NATALIE: Yes.

[05:52] DAVE: The center might benefit the town of Horton. At present, the town feels almost deserted. Once young residents leave school and gain skills or qualifications, they move to the city for employment. The population left behind consists mainly of children and retired people.

[06:10] NATALIE: Another area to investigate is the environmental damage that additional tourists might cause. Visitors can currently walk anywhere around the site. If numbers rise, restrictions may be necessary, such as requiring everyone to remain on marked paths. Guides and wardens would have to ensure that people followed the rules.
[06:35] DAVE: Yes, we should include that. All right, well.

content: 📌 The effects of environmental change on birds
Mercury (Hg)
is extremely poisonousenters the atmosphere when coal is burnedcan be consumed by fish after reaching waterhas recently been shown to affect birds that eat [ _____ ]

Research into mercury’s effects on birds
Claire Varian-Ramos is studying:
changes in birds’ [ _____ ] and mental processes such as memory changes in birdsong, which young birds normally learn from their [ _____ ]
Findings:
exposure to mercury results in songs that are less [ _____ ].this may lower successful [ _____ ].
Laboratory studies:
provide researchers with greater [ _____ ].
Implications for humans

Migratory birds such as [ _____ ] may contain mercury and later be eaten.Mercury may interfere with the learning of [ _____ ].Mercury entering a mother’s body through [ _____ ] may harm her unborn child.Regulations controlling mercury emissions will increase everyone’s energy [ _____ ].
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecturer discussing how mercury pollution affects birds and may also affect humans. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. We've been considering how human changes to the environment influence wildlife.

[00:58] AUDIO: I'll now focus on one example, mercury. Mercury is one of roughly 120 elements that make up matter, and its chemical symbol is Hg. It is a shiny silver-colored substance that you may remember from traditional thermometers. It is rarely used in the home now because it is extremely toxic.

[01:23] AUDIO: Unfortunately, mercury levels in the environment are rising. Electricity-generating power stations are the main cause because most continue to burn coal, releasing mercury into the air. Some eventually settles in rivers and lakes. When a fish consumes it, the mercury remains in its body and enters the food chain.

[01:48] AUDIO: Scientists have long understood the risk to fish-eating birds. More recent evidence shows that birds whose diet consists of insects can also be harmed. Claire Varian Ramos is conducting research into these effects. Instead of simply counting birds killed by mercury poisoning, she is examining less obvious consequences.

[02:13] AUDIO: These include changes in behavior and in mental processes such as memory. Her main interest is the effect on bird song. Birds learn to sing at a particular stage of development. A young bird appears to acquire its song by listening to its father rather than to other birds.

[02:35] AUDIO: Varian Ramos has already found that young males exposed to mercury through contaminated food produce songs that are less complex than those of unexposed birds. Even limited exposure made their form matter in the wild. Simpler songs can make males less attractive to females and reduce their chances of reproduction. Her research combines laboratory experiments with outdoor studies of wild birds.

[03:08] AUDIO: Laboratory work removes many of the variables present in a natural environment, giving the researcher far greater control. This can increase confidence in the findings, and researchers also avoid the difficulty of locating birds in the wild before observing them. What does this mean for people? Because many bird species migrate, they can carry mercury far beyond the original polluted site.

[03:37] AUDIO: Ducks that had fed in a contaminated area, for example, were later shot by hunters more than a thousand kilometers away and were probably eaten. Their mercury levels were high enough to raise concerns about human consumption. Returning to song learning, mercury contamination can disrupt this process in birds. Among humans, mercury is also known to delay children's acquisition of language.

[04:07] AUDIO: The learning process involves similar regions of the brain and even some of the same genes. There are further consequences for people. An unborn child may be harmed when food eaten by its mother contains a high concentration of mercury, and the effects can be considerable. Ultimately, the debate concerns the relative value placed on economic well-being and environmental protection.

[04:35] AUDIO: New rules limiting mercury emissions from power plants will cost billions of dollars to introduce and will raise energy costs for everyone. Some people argue that this is too high a price for protecting wildlife, but the effects extend beyond wildlife, so the issue requires very careful consideration.

[00:52] BOB: Hello, Pembroke Cycling Holidays, Bob speaking.
[00:56] MARGARET: Hello, I noticed your advertisement for cycle trip leaders. Am I speaking to the person who deals with applications?
[01:06] BOB: Yes, you are. Could you tell me your name?
[01:10] MARGARET: Margaret Smith.
[01:12] BOB: Thanks. Are you hoping to find permanent work, Margaret?
[01:16] MARGARET: No, something temporary. I've got a permanent post beginning in a few months, so I'd like another job until then.
[01:24] BOB: What sort of work are you in?
[01:26] MARGARET: It may sound rather odd. I used to practice law, but I changed career completely. I've just completed my training, and I'll soon be working as a doctor.
[01:39] BOB: I see. Have you ever been in charge of cycling tours?
[01:44] MARGARET: Yes. I've led several cycle trips in Africa. I was due to lead one in India next month, but that was cancelled. So your advertisement came at the right time.

[01:58] BOB: Good. We generally send two or three leaders, depending on the group size. Some trips are aimed at highly experienced cyclists. However, a tour in Spain has attracted so much interest that we need one more leader.
[02:14] BOB: It's a cycling holiday for families. Would you be interested?
[02:19] MARGARET: Very much. I like working with children. And I'd prefer to gain more experience before taking on a really demanding trip.
[02:30] BOB: There'll be several teenagers on that holiday. Have you worked with people of that age?
[02:36] MARGARET: Yes. At present, I volunteer at a youth club, helping members improve their cycling. Before that, I helped at a cycling club where I taught beginners.
[02:48] BOB: Excellent. The trip I've described lasts only two weeks, though there may be other tours for you to lead afterwards. Would that suit your plans?
[02:58] MARGARET: Yes. I'm available for five months. My new job starts on the 2nd of October, so I can work from the 1st of May until near the end of September.
[03:10] BOB: Fine. Is there anything we should know about your diet? We often have participants who don't eat meat or who have food allergies, so we take care with that.
[03:22] MARGARET: I am allergic to cheese. Would that cause any difficulty?
[03:27] BOB: No. If we know beforehand, we can make suitable arrangements.
[03:33] MARGARET: That's reassuring.
[03:38] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.
[04:24] MARGARET: This sounds very interesting. Shall I complete an application form?
[04:29] BOB: Yes, please. What address should I send it to?
[04:33] MARGARET: Please post it to 27 Arbuthnot Place, Dumfries. That's A-R-B-U-T-H-N-O-T.
[04:43] BOB: And the postcode?
[04:44] MARGARET: D-G-74-P-H.
[04:47] BOB: Is that P for Papa or B for Bravo?
[04:51] MARGARET: P for Papa.
[04:52] BOB: Got it. If you send the completed form back by this Friday, we can interview you next Tuesday at half-past two. Can you make that?
[05:02] MARGARET: Yes, that's fine. You are quite a distance from me, so I'll drive over on Monday. Is there anything I should take to the interview?
[05:13] BOB: We'll already have the form. Please bring any relevant certificates you hold, in cycling, first aid or similar areas.
[05:22] MARGARET: All right.

[05:23] BOB: We'd also like to hear about your experience as a tour guide. Could you prepare a 10-minute presentation on that? There is no need for slides or other equipment. A few notes will be enough.
[05:36] MARGARET: Certainly. I'll begin planning it straight away.
[05:40] BOB: Good. We look forward to receiving your form and we'll contact you to confirm the interview.
[05:47] MARGARET: Thank you very much.
[05:48] BOB: Thank you, Margaret. Goodbye.
[05:51] MARGARET: Goodbye.

content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Visiting Sheepmarket Area"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a podcast about the sheep market area of a city. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Welcome to this podcast about the sheep market, one of the city's oldest districts.

[00:54] AUDIO: The name comes from the market where farmers once sold sheep. Since then, the area has been redeveloped into a lively neighbourhood and it now contains one of the city's fastest expanding communities. The nearby university has always brought in students for the nightlife. More recently, however, young graduates starting careers in fashion and design have been purchasing the new flats.

[01:24] AUDIO: Those flats replaced the small homes formerly occupied by market employees. Away from the main roads, the sheep market has a network of narrow side streets that are well worth exploring. These old lanes are excellent places to find one-off paintings, handcrafted jewellery and pottery at affordable prices, as well as locally grown fruit and vegetables. There are also plenty of pavement cafes where you can sit with a drink and watch visitors from around the world.

[02:00] AUDIO: By contrast, the area's oldest buildings are mostly found on the main roads, including the city's first department store. It dates from the 1880s and is still trading today. The sheep market is also an important fashion centre and there is a deliberate effort to support new designers. The Young Fashion Competition is for local young people with a strong interest in the subject.

[02:29] AUDIO: This year, their outfit must draw on the music and technology found in present-day life. They may use natural or synthetic fibres. A panel of specialists and designers will assess the clothes and models will wear the winning designs at a special gala. Parking in the sheep market is straightforward.

[02:52] AUDIO: Roadside pay and display spaces are suitable for a visit of an hour or two. For a full day, one of the four underground car parks is a better option. Charges are modest and shoppers who show a receipt from a local shop pay nothing. After six in the evening, many car parks use a single fixed charge, which varies but is generally reasonable.

[03:23] AUDIO: Before you hear the rest of the podcast, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now, listen and answer questions 15 to 20. The sheep market is among the country's leading areas for art and history. Now, if you look at the map, you can see several of its principal attractions.

[04:19] AUDIO: Visitors usually begin on Crawley Road at the bottom. Starting there, Reynolds House, one of the city's oldest homes, is open to visitors. It stands on the north side of Crawley Road, beside the path going towards the public gardens. Moving on, the district is especially well known for its unusual sculptures.

[04:44] AUDIO: One of the most striking is the thumb, which is shaped exactly as its name suggests, although it is roughly 10 metres tall. To find it, go to Hill Road, where it stands directly opposite the bank. Now, if we move over to the eastern side of the sheep market, you'll find the museum. Which has an excellent collection of landscapes from New Zealand.

[05:12] AUDIO: It is on City Road, facing the public gardens from across the road, and immediately opposite the junction with Hill Road. From there, let's move on to the Contemporary Art Gallery. You reach it by taking a short street leading away from Station Square, close to the public gardens. You'll know you're on the right road because it finishes at the gallery rather than continuing beyond it.

[05:41] AUDIO: The gallery is open every day, apart from Monday. Next, we have the Warner Gallery, which concentrates on 19th century art. You'll find this on City Road, near the Crawley Road junction, on the same side as the public gardens. It opens from 9 to 5 on weekdays, and there is no admission charge.

[06:09] AUDIO: And finally, if you're interested in buying high-quality art, you should visit Nucleus. To get there, start from Crawley Road. Go through Station Square, and head east along Hill Road, until you come to a small curving road branching off. Take that turning and follow the road, and you'll find Nucleus on your right.
[06:34] AUDIO: Just remember, if you reach City Road, you've gone past the turning. That is the end of part two. You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

content: Stage of the presentationPreparation still requiredExplain Giannetti's book, which gives a [ _____ ] of adaptationsPut existing notes in orderInvite the class to identify the [ _____ ] adaptationsNothing furtherOutline Rachel Malchow's ideasCreate some [ _____ ]Examine the connection between adaptations and contemporary [ _____ ] when a film is madeNothing further
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two film studies students discussing a presentation about screen versions of Shakespeare's plays. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:53] KATIE: Joe, you know I've got to give a presentation in our film studies class next week?
[00:59] JOE: Yes.
[01:01] KATIE: Could I talk it through with you? I'd really value another person's view.
[01:08] JOE: Certainly, Katie. What's the subject?
[01:12] KATIE: Film adaptations of Shakespeare's plays. I've become fascinated by the very different methods directors use.
[01:19] JOE: Right.

[01:21] KATIE: I plan to begin with Janetti, the professor of film and literature. In one of his books, he proposes a simple classification of adaptations according to how closely they follow the plays or novels on which they're based. I've taken notes already, so I only need to put them into a sensible order. After that, I thought I'd ask the class to name the worst Shakespeare adaptations they've watched and explain their choices.
[01:51] KATIE: That could be more entertaining than asking about favorites.
[01:55] JOE: I'm sure I can think of two or three.
[01:58] KATIE: Then I'd like to cover Rachel Malkow. I found material online about her work on film adaptation, and my first idea was to show clips that demonstrate her arguments.
[02:11] JOE: Would you have time to prepare all that and show it during the session? You may not even be able to locate every extract you need.
[02:20] KATIE: That's probably true. In that case, I'll make some slides instead, explaining how different films connect with her ideas. They should still generate discussion.
[02:32] JOE: Yes.
[02:33] KATIE: Next, I want to examine how a play may be selected for adaptation, because it deals with issues that matter at the time the film is produced.
[02:43] JOE: Do you mean subjects such as patriotism or the part played by government?
[02:47] KATIE: Exactly. It's a difficult area, but I have several ideas for the class to discuss.
[02:58] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
[03:44] KATIE: Finally, I'll discuss several adaptations that demonstrate a range of approaches and give my views on them. Have you seen the Japanese film Ran?
[03:55] JOE: No, I haven't. It's based on King Lear, isn't it?

[03:59] KATIE: Yes. It follows the same basic situation and plot quite freely, but transfers the action from 16th century Britain to 16th century Japan. For instance, the king's daughters become sons because women in Japanese society at that time could not inherit the throne.
[04:18] JOE: I hope you'll include the 1993 version of Much Ado About Nothing. For me, it's one of the finest Shakespeare films. It makes the play feel very immediate.
[04:32] KATIE: I agree. Shooting it in Italy, the play's own setting, also gives a clear impression of life in the period when the story takes place.
[04:42] JOE: Definitely. Which film comes next?
[04:45] KATIE: The 1996 Romeo and Juliet, which relocates the action to the modern day.
[04:53] JOE: That worked extremely well. The two feuding families became rival business dynasties, although the actors still use Shakespeare's original English.
[05:03] KATIE: You might expect that combination to sound strange, but I adjusted to it very quickly.
[05:10] JOE: So did I.
[05:11] KATIE: Then I'll use an example of a genuine Hollywood production designed for a large commercial audience.
[05:19] JOE: There must be plenty to choose from.

[05:21] KATIE: There are, but I've selected the 1996 Hamlet. It keeps every line of the text, yet it feels too much like a standard action hero movie. There are numerous special effects, but no single interpretation holding the play together.
[05:40] JOE: So the spectacle overwhelms the meaning.
[05:43] KATIE: Precisely. After that comes Prospero's books, adapted from the Tempest. Its style was highly original.
[05:53] JOE: Didn't it combine live acting with dance, song, and animation?
[05:58] KATIE: It did. I also want to include Looking for Richard. Have you seen that one?
[06:04] JOE: No, though I've read about it. Wasn't it a documentary mixed with a small number of scenes from Richard III?

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecture about the study and design of sound in cities. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. This lecture looks at acoustics, the science of sound in urban settings such as cities.

[01:00] AUDIO: As an acoustic engineer, I believe this field is likely to change considerably. Earlier research into city soundscapes was quite basic. We recorded sound levels in decibels. I might take a meter to a particular location, measure the noise, and then ask a group of people at what point they found it irritating.

[01:25] AUDIO: Information of this kind allowed acoustic engineers to produce what are known as noise maps, showing the sound environment. In reality though, these maps have limited value. They reveal that roads generally have the greatest noise levels, which is hardly unexpected. They miss a great deal because they cannot represent the complicated changes in sound over time.

[01:55] AUDIO: For example, they leave out noise coming through neighbours' open windows, or from neighbours spending time in their gardens, which can be quite noticeable in summer. No database records that kind of information. The maps also fail to reflect individual differences in the way noise is perceived. Someone like me, after years in acoustics, may react very differently from someone without that experience.

[02:27] AUDIO: Even so, these fairly rough maps have helped by supplying information and making the public aware that noise needs attention. In other words, it is a political issue. That recognition matters because rules and regulations are needed. Noise can produce a range of harmful effects.

[02:51] AUDIO: People who live in cities know that activity continues around the clock, so disturbed sleep is common. We also know that noise can raise stress levels through physical changes that affect the blood. There are further consequences. If school children lack a quiet place to study, the quality of their work is likely to decline.

[03:17] AUDIO: A further weakness of measuring decibels is that the figure does not distinguish one kind of noise from another. Sounds that many people regard as pleasant and calming may still register quite high readings. Consider, for example, a fountain in a town square. We would not necessarily want to limit or remove that sound.

[03:43] AUDIO: Researchers may therefore need to take such sounds into account in urban design. But decibel readings alone cannot do this. Instead, many investigators are adopting methods from the social sciences, including questionnaires that explore people's emotional reactions to sound. So what would people actually like to hear in a city?

[04:12] AUDIO: Recent research involving several disciplines has produced findings that initially appear inconsistent. Urban areas need a feeling of activity. They should be lively, with noises such as heels clicking on paving or steam hissing from a coffee machine. At the same time, those sounds must not become intrusive because people also need opportunities to unwind.

[04:43] AUDIO: A major obstacle will be persuading architects and town planners to apply this research. Beyond a basic introduction to acoustics, they receive very little training in the subject. They should view sound as a way of enriching urban life. At present, however, they often treat it as something to eliminate or minimise, or as an engineering responsibility comparable to street drainage.

[05:16] AUDIO: City noise needs to be understood as an aesthetic feature, possessing qualities associated with an art form. Once we accept that, we must investigate what shapes it and how designers can use it. This calls for a sophisticated understanding of several factors. How does sound relate to culture?

[05:42] AUDIO: What can psychology tell us about its interaction with human development and social relationships, and about its influence on thoughts and feelings? Can physics help us understand the nature of sound itself? Modern technology may also assist. Architects and planners already use virtual reality programs to communicate their ideas and demonstrate the likely effect of proposed buildings.

[06:16] AUDIO: The current problem is that these programs are silent. In future, realistic audio could be added, allowing soundscapes to be tested before construction. With the best available technology, the future city may be as satisfying to hear as it is to see.
